label: June 2026 paper — gap-fill practice variants (booklet Q1–Q50)

items.stem: X = (X₁, X₂, X₃, X₄)′ has E(X) = 0 and a covariance matrix Σ with 1 on the diagonal and 1/3 everywhere else. Consider: A. The first principal component is (1/2)(X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄). B. The largest eigenvalue of Σ is 2. C. The first principal component explains 50% of the total variability. D. The smallest eigenvalue of Σ is 1/3. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: An equicorrelation matrix with p = 4 and ρ = 1/3 has eigenvalues 1 + 3ρ = 2 (once, eigenvector (1, 1, 1, 1)/2) and 1 − ρ = 2/3 (three times). The total variance is 4, so the first component explains 2/4 = 50%. The smallest eigenvalue is 2/3, not ρ. Trap: the eigenvalues are 1 + (p − 1)ρ and 1 − ρ, not ρ itself.

items.stem: X = (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄)′ has E(X) = 0 and Σ = [[1, 0, 0.6, 0], [0, 1, 0, 0.3], [0.6, 0, 1, 0], [0, 0.3, 0, 1]]. With x⁽¹⁾ = (x₁, x₂)′ and x⁽²⁾ = (x₃, x₄)′, the largest canonical correlation between x⁽¹⁾ and x⁽²⁾ is
items.explanation: Here Σ₁₁ = Σ₂₂ = I and Σ₁₂ = diag(0.6, 0.3), so the squared canonical correlations are the eigenvalues of Σ₁₂Σ₂₂⁻¹Σ₂₁Σ₁₁⁻¹ = diag(0.36, 0.09). The largest canonical correlation is √0.36 = 0.60. Trap: 0.36 is its square, and 0.45 averages the two correlations.
